title: if and if-else
summary: Master binary decision-making: executing mutually exclusive blocks with if-else, curly braces best practices, and avoiding dead code.
learningObjectives: Implement mutually exclusive binary execution paths using if-else
Understand why curly braces { } are essential even for single-line statements
Trace execution flow through true and false branches
Solve classic binary decision problems: pass/fail, even/odd, and admission status
expectedOutcomes: Write clean, readable binary branching code without syntax ambiguity
Avoid single-statement bracket omission bugs in team codebases

activities.title: Mutually Exclusive Branching: if-else

breakdown.whatIsIt: A binary branching structure guaranteeing that exactly one of two blocks runs based on condition truth.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Binary decisions are the most fundamental building block in all computer programming.
howItWorks: If the condition evaluates to true, the if block runs.
If the condition evaluates to false, the else block runs.
Control never enters both blocks in the same execution.
Omitting curly braces attaches only the single immediate statement to the branch.
keyTakeaways: Always use curly braces { } even for single-line statements.
Visual indentation does not control Java block scope; braces do.
Use if-else when there are two strictly complementary outcomes.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: ATM Cash Withdrawal Check
activities.description: Notice how the program executes either the success branch or the declined branch, updating account state only when the condition is satisfied.

questions.prompt: In an if-else statement, is it possible for both the if block and the else block to execute during the same run?
options: Yes, if the condition changes while executing
No, they are mutually exclusive; exactly one will run
Yes, if multiple threads are running
Only if the condition is null
questions.explanation: By definition, if-else guarantees mutual exclusivity. A condition evaluates to either true or false at the decision point; therefore, exactly one block executes.
hints: Can a boolean be both true and false at the same moment?

questions.explanation: 7 % 2 is 1 (not equal to 0). The condition is false, so control jumps to the else block, printing 'Odd'.
hints: 7 divided by 2 has a remainder of 1.

options: notifyAdmin() will execute unconditionally every time, regardless of auth
notifyAdmin() is treated as an else branch
questions.explanation: Without braces, only the single statement 'login();' belongs to the if block. 'notifyAdmin();' is a separate subsequent statement that executes unconditionally.
hints: Indentation does not create blocks in Java.

questions.prompt: Can an else block exist in Java without a preceding if statement?
options: Yes, if placed at the end of the file
No, 'else without if' is a compilation error
questions.explanation: An 'else' block must immediately follow an 'if' (or 'else if') block. An isolated 'else' produces the compiler error 'else without if'.
hints: Every else must belong to an if.

questions.explanation: These are two separate statements: The first 'if (x > 10)' is true, printing 'High '. The second 'if (x > 15)' is also true, printing 'Ultra '. Total: 'High Ultra '.
hints: Notice the first if does not have an else.

questions.prompt: What happens if a variable is declared inside an if block: 'if (true) { int y = 5; }'?
options: y is accessible anywhere in the method
y is scoped only to that if block and cannot be accessed outside it
y is stored in the heap
questions.explanation: Variables declared inside curly braces { } have block scope. They are allocated in the stack frame and destroyed when the block ends.

questions.prompt: Which ternary expression is equivalent to: if (x >= 0) sign = 1; else sign = -1;?

questions.explanation: 0 > 0 is false. 0 < 0 is false. Control falls through to the final else block, printing 'Z' for zero.
hints: Zero is neither positive nor negative.

options: Compilation error: variable declaration not allowed here
questions.explanation: In Java, a variable declaration is not allowed as the single unbraced statement of an if or else branch. Without braces, the variable would instantly go out of scope, so Java forbids it.
hints: A variable declared without braces would have no scope to exist.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: if-else Mechanics

interviewQA.question: Why is it considered a major code smell to omit curly braces in if-else statements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Omitting curly braces is dangerous because indentation is ignored by the Java compiler. If another developer adds a second statement intended to be inside the condition, only the first line is conditionally bound, while the second line executes unconditionally. The infamous Apple SSL 'goto fail' security vulnerability was caused by an unbraced conditional flaw. Industry style guides (Google, Oracle) mandate braces for all conditional blocks.
keyPoints: Always use braces; unbraced conditionals cause silent logic bugs during code maintenance.

interviewQA.question: Why cannot a variable declaration be the only statement in an unbraced if block?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Writing `if (condition) int x = 10;` is a compile error because the scope of `x` would end at the end of that single statement. Because `x` could never be referenced anywhere else in the code, the Java language specification forbids variable declarations without an enclosing block `{ ... }`.
keyPoints: Variable declarations require an enclosing block so the variable has a meaningful scope.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between if-else and the ternary operator (? :)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `if-else` is a **control-flow statement** used to execute blocks of code; it does not produce a value. The ternary operator (`? :`) is an **expression** that evaluates to a value and can be assigned directly to a variable or passed as a method argument.
keyPoints: if-else is a statement for controlling execution; ternary is an expression that yields a value.

interviewQA.question: Can you have an if statement inside an else block?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. Writing `else if (condition)` is syntactically just an `else` block whose single statement is another `if`. Java's formatted indentation makes it read like a unified `else-if` ladder.
keyPoints: else if is syntactically an if nested immediately inside an else.

interviewQA.question: What is the 'Dangling Else' problem in programming languages?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: When multiple nested `if` statements are followed by a single `else`, ambiguity can arise about which `if` the `else` belongs to. In Java, the rule is unambiguous: an `else` **always pairs with the closest preceding unclosed `if`** in the same block.
keyPoints: An else always binds to the closest preceding unclosed if in the same scope.

interviewQA.question: How does branch prediction optimize if-else chains?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The CPU's Branch Target Buffer (BTB) records historical branches taken. If an `if` branch is taken 99% of the time, the CPU speculatively executes the instructions inside that branch before the comparison finishes. If the condition is verified, zero clock cycles are wasted.
keyPoints: CPUs speculatively execute likely branches to keep execution pipelines saturated.

interviewQA.question: When should you prefer early return over an if-else block?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: When validating preconditions (error states, null checks, boundary violations), using early return (`if (!valid) return;`) flattens the code structure, reducing visual indentation and cyclomatic complexity compared to deeply nested `if-else` blocks.
keyPoints: Early return flattens code and isolates error handling from the main business logic.

interviewQA.question: What is dead code in conditional statements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Dead code refers to statements that can never be executed under any circumstances (e.g. `if (false) { ... }`). The Java compiler analyzes unreachable code and will issue a compilation error: `unreachable code`.
keyPoints: Unreachable code caused by constant false conditions triggers compile errors in Java.
